topics.title: Japan and South Korea as emerging powers

learn.hook: Your family car might be a Suzuki or Hyundai, your TV a Sony or Samsung. Two East Asian nations built global brands from post-war ruins.
points: Japan has few natural resources and imports most raw materials, yet it became a leading economic and technological power, with brands like Sony, Panasonic, Canon, Toyota, Honda and Suzuki. It is a member of the G-7 (formerly G-8).

Japan is the only country to have suffered nuclear bombing (Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 1945). Article 9 of its Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right, so its military role is limited. Japan is one of the largest contributors to the UN budget.

South Korea grew rapidly from the 1960s to the 1980s. This rise is called the 'Miracle on the Han River'. Factors included land reform, rural development, investment in human resources and rapid industrialisation.
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996 and is a member of the G-20. Its global brands include Samsung, LG and Hyundai.
Comparing centres of power: the EU and ASEAN are regional groups that pool members' strength, while China, Japan and South Korea are individual states that rose through economic growth.

example.q: Board-style: Give two reasons why Japan is considered an important centre of power.
steps: Economic and technological strength with global brands, despite few natural resources.
Major contributor to the UN budget and member of the G-7.
(Its military role is limited by Article 9.)
example.answer: Strong technology-based economy; major UN funder and G-7 member

learn.reallife: Japan has funded the Delhi Metro and the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project, while Korean firms like Hyundai and Samsung run big factories in Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh.

Articles 51 and 370 are linked to other texts, not Japan.
So Article 9.
Answer: Article 9
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Indian constitutional articles

quiz.q: Japan is the only country to have suffered:
quiz.explain: Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.
steps: Fact: Japan is the only country to have suffered nuclear bombing.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.
So destruction by nuclear bombs.
Answer: Destruction by nuclear bombs
quiz.mistake: Confuses Japan with Korea or Germany

quiz.q: The term 'Miracle on the Han River' refers to:
quiz.explain: It describes South Korea's fast industrial rise.
steps: Fact: South Korea's rapid growth from the 1960s to 1980s is called the 'Miracle on the Han River'.
It is not about Japan or China.
So South Korea's rapid economic growth.
Answer: South Korea's rapid economic growth

quiz.q: South Korea became a member of the OECD in:
quiz.explain: It joined the OECD in 1996.
steps: Fact: South Korea joined the OECD in 1996.
1991 is the year both Koreas joined the UN, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 1996
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the year both Koreas joined the UN (1991)

quiz.q: Which is true of Japan's natural resources?
options: It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials
It is the world's largest oil exporter
It has the largest coal reserves in Asia
It needs no imports at all
quiz.explain: Japan's power rests on technology and industry, not natural resources.
steps: Fact: Japan has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
Its power rests on technology and industry.
So it has few natural resources and imports most raw materials.
Answer: It has few natural resources and imports most raw materials
quiz.mistake: Assumes economic power needs natural resources

quiz.q: Which factor helped South Korea's rapid development?
options: Land reform and investment in human resources
quiz.explain: Land reform, rural development, human resources and industrialisation fuelled growth.
steps: Fact: South Korea's growth came from land reform, rural development, human resources and industrialisation.
Isolation or rejecting industry would slow growth.
So land reform and investment in human resources.
Answer: Land reform and investment in human resources
quiz.mistake: Picks factors that would slow growth

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Japan's military role is limited. Reason (R): Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution renounces war as a sovereign right.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; Article 9 explains the limited military role.
steps: A: true — Japan's military role is limited.
R: true — Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right.
R explains A: the constitution limits its military role.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the constitutional clause with military limits

quiz.q: Case: A class compares the EU with Japan as 'centres of power'. Which difference is correct?
options: The EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state
The EU has one army and Japan has none
quiz.explain: The EU pools many states' strength, whereas Japan is one country that rose through its economy.
steps: The EU is a regional group that pools the strength of many states.
Japan is one country that rose through economic growth.
So the EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state.
Answer: The EU is a regional union of states; Japan is a single state
quiz.mistake: Treats a country and a regional union as the same kind of actor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Japan and South Korea are small. How can they be centres of power?'
teach.praise: Yay! Japan and South Korea built mighty economies and technology. Japan's military is limited by Article 9, and Korea had its Han River miracle!
teach.nudge: Good. What limits Japan's military? And what is South Korea's growth story called?

revise.summary: Japan, with few natural resources, became a leading technological economy and big UN funder, with a military limited by Article 9. South Korea's rapid rise, the 'Miracle on the Han River', came from land reform, human resources and industrialisation; it joined the OECD in 1996.
focus: Why Japan is a centre of power
How states differ from regional unions as centres of power
remember: Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right
Japan: only country to suffer nuclear bombing (1945)
South Korea joined the OECD in 1996
traps: The 'Miracle on the Han River' is South Korea, not Japan.
Economic power does not need natural resources.
Japan is a single state, the EU a regional union.

topics.title: What is South Asia?

learn.hook: One mountain range, one ocean, and around a quarter of humanity in between. South Asia is a region of shared geography but very different political systems.
points: South Asia usually includes Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan and Myanmar are often included in discussions of the region.
Geography gives the region a natural unity: the Himalayas in the north, the Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal to the south, west and east.

Politically the region is very diverse: India and Sri Lanka have kept democratic systems since independence, Pakistan and Bangladesh have alternated between civilian and military rule, Nepal moved from monarchy to a republic, and Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.

Map work: Islamabad (Pakistan), Dhaka (Bangladesh), Kathmandu (Nepal), Thimphu (Bhutan), Malé (the Maldives), New Delhi (India), Kabul (Afghanistan). Sri Lanka's official capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, with Colombo as its commercial capital.

example.q: A map question asks you to mark the capitals of three Himalayan neighbours of India. Name them.
steps: Nepal: Kathmandu.
Bhutan: Thimphu.
Pakistan: Islamabad (its north lies in the Himalaya-Karakoram region).
example.answer: Kathmandu, Thimphu, Islamabad

learn.reallife: The monsoon that waters Indian farms also feeds rivers flowing through Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. Shared rivers and weather tie the region together.

games.title: Democratic all along, or mixed record?
buckets: Alternated between democracy and non-democratic rule

quiz.q: Which of these is the capital of Bhutan?
quiz.explain: Thimphu is Bhutan's capital; Kathmandu is Nepal's.
steps: Asked: Bhutan's capital.
Fact: Thimphu is the capital of Bhutan.
Kathmandu is Nepal's, Dhaka Bangladesh's and Malé the Maldives'.
Answer: Thimphu

quiz.q: Which country is NOT usually counted in the core list of South Asian countries?
quiz.explain: Indonesia is in Southeast Asia and belongs to ASEAN.
steps: Core South Asia: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka.
Indonesia is in Southeast Asia and belongs to ASEAN.
So Indonesia is NOT in the core list.
Answer: Indonesia
quiz.mistake: Confuses South Asia with Southeast Asia

quiz.q: Which two countries are often included in discussions of South Asia besides the seven core countries?
quiz.explain: Afghanistan and Myanmar are frequently discussed as part of the region.
steps: Fact: Afghanistan and Myanmar are often included in discussions of South Asia.
China, Japan, Iran, Thailand and Vietnam belong to other regions.
So Afghanistan and Myanmar.
Answer: Afghanistan and Myanmar

quiz.q: The capital of the Maldives is:
quiz.explain: Malé is the capital of the island nation of the Maldives.
steps: Fact: Malé is the capital of the Maldives.
Colombo is Sri Lanka's commercial capital; Thimphu is Bhutan's.
So Malé.
Answer: Malé
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Sri Lanka's commercial capital

quiz.q: Which natural feature forms South Asia's northern boundary?
quiz.explain: The Himalayas lie to the north; seas and the ocean lie to the south.
steps: Fact: the Himalayas lie to the north of South Asia.
The Indian Ocean and seas lie to the south, west and east.
So the Himalayas.
Answer: The Himalayas

quiz.q: Which statement about political systems in South Asia is correct?
options: All countries have always been monarchies
They are diverse: democracies, monarchies and periods of military rule
All countries have always been military dictatorships
All have the same constitution as India
quiz.explain: The region has a wide variety of political systems.
steps: India and Sri Lanka stayed democratic; Pakistan and Bangladesh had military rule.
Nepal became a republic; Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.
So the systems are diverse: democracies, monarchies and periods of military rule.
Answer: They are diverse: democracies, monarchies and periods of military rule
quiz.mistake: Assumes a single system for the whole region

quiz.q: Assertion (A): South Asia has a distinctive geographic unity. Reason (R): It is bounded by the Himalayas in the north and by seas and the Indian Ocean in the south.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the natural boundaries give the region its unity.
steps: A: true — South Asia has a natural geographic unity.
R: true — Himalayas in the north, seas and Indian Ocean to the south.
R explains A: these natural boundaries create the unity.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to link physical boundaries with regional unity

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India and Sri Lanka have remained democracies since independence. Reason (R): Bhutan is a republic with no king.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy.
steps: A: true — India and Sri Lanka have stayed democratic since independence.
R: false — Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy, not a republic.
So A is true, but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'Which countries are in South Asia? And are they all run the same way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Seven core countries, tied by the Himalayas and the ocean, but each with very different politics!
teach.nudge: Can you name the countries and tell me if they all have the same kind of government?

revise.summary: South Asia's core is Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, often with Afghanistan and Myanmar. The Himalayas and the seas give it geographic unity, but its political systems are diverse.
focus: Countries and capitals of South Asia
remember: Thimphu (Bhutan), Kathmandu (Nepal), Malé (Maldives), Dhaka, Islamabad, Kabul
Sri Lanka: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte official, Colombo commercial
Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy; Nepal is now a republic
traps: Indonesia is Southeast Asia, not South Asia.
Don't mix up Thimphu and Kathmandu.
Bhutan is not a republic.

topics.title: The military and democracy in Pakistan

learn.hook: Pakistan's history reads like a relay race between generals and elected leaders, with the baton changing hands again and again.
points: After Pakistan framed its first constitution, General Ayub Khan took over in 1958 and soon got himself elected. Popular dissatisfaction forced him out, and General Yahya Khan took over in 1969.

After the 1971 war, an elected government under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto ruled from 1971 to 1977. General Zia-ul-Haq removed it in 1977. A pro-democracy movement led to an elected government under Benazir Bhutto in 1988.

Elected governments of Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif followed. In 1999 the army under General Pervez Musharraf took over again. Since 2008 elected civilian governments have ruled, but the army keeps great influence.

Reasons for weak democracy: the social dominance of the military, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy; conflict with India strengthening pro-military groups; and support for military rule from the USA and others during the Cold War.

example.q: Order these leaders in Pakistan's history: Zia-ul-Haq, Ayub Khan, Pervez Musharraf, Benazir Bhutto.
steps: Ayub Khan: took over in 1958.
Zia-ul-Haq: took over in 1977.
Benazir Bhutto: elected in 1988.
Pervez Musharraf: took over in 1999.
example.answer: Ayub Khan → Zia-ul-Haq → Benazir Bhutto → Pervez Musharraf

learn.reallife: When Indian and Pakistani teams meet at cricket, commentators often note how differently the two countries' institutions evolved after 1947, even though both started from the same colonial system.

quiz.q: Who took over Pakistan's administration in 1958?
quiz.explain: Ayub Khan's takeover in 1958 began military rule.
steps: Fact: General Ayub Khan took over in 1958 after the first constitution.
Zia (1977) and Musharraf (1999) came later.
So General Ayub Khan.
Answer: General Ayub Khan

quiz.q: Which general removed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government in 1977?
quiz.explain: General Zia-ul-Haq took over in 1977.
steps: Fact: Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's elected government ruled 1971–1977.
General Zia-ul-Haq removed it in 1977.
Yahya Khan was 1969 and Musharraf 1999, so Zia-ul-Haq.
Answer: Zia-ul-Haq
quiz.mistake: Confuses the order of military rulers

quiz.q: In 1988, a democratically elected government came to power in Pakistan under:
quiz.explain: Benazir Bhutto led the government elected in 1988.
steps: Fact: a pro-democracy movement led to an elected government in 1988.
It was led by Benazir Bhutto; Nawaz Sharif came later.
So Benazir Bhutto.
Answer: Benazir Bhutto
quiz.mistake: Picks Nawaz Sharif, who came later

quiz.q: The army took over in Pakistan again in 1999 under:
quiz.explain: Musharraf removed the elected government in 1999.
steps: Fact: in 1999 the army took over again.
It was led by General Pervez Musharraf.
Yahya Khan and Zia ruled earlier, so Musharraf.
Answer: General Pervez Musharraf

quiz.q: Which is a reason for the failure of democracy to take firm root in Pakistan?
options: Social dominance of the military, clergy and landowning aristocracy
A strong tradition of independent courts and free press from the start
Too many free and fair elections
quiz.explain: These groups dominated society and weakened democratic institutions.
steps: Fact: one reason democracy stayed weak was the social dominance of powerful groups.
These were the military, the clergy and the landowning aristocracy.
So the social dominance of the military, clergy and landowning aristocracy.
Answer: Social dominance of the military, clergy and landowning aristocracy
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the power of the army and elites

quiz.q: How did the Cold War affect democracy in Pakistan?
options: The USA and others backed military rulers for their own strategic interests
The USA forced Pakistan to remain a monarchy
The Cold War had no link with Pakistan
quiz.explain: Outside powers tolerated or supported military regimes that served their interests.
steps: Fact: during the Cold War the USA and others supported military rule in Pakistan.
They did so for their own strategic interests.
So outside powers backed military rulers.
Answer: The USA and others backed military rulers for their own strategic interests
quiz.mistake: Ignores the role of external support

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pro-military groups in Pakistan became stronger over time. Reason (R): Pakistan's conflicts with India made the army's role seem more important.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; tension with India strengthened arguments for military influence.
steps: A: true — pro-military groups became stronger.
R: true — conflict with India made the army seem more important.
R explains A: the conflict strengthened pro-military groups.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to link external conflict with internal military power

quiz.q: Case: A Pakistani elected government holds office, but major decisions on defence and foreign policy are shaped by army generals. Which feature of Pakistan's politics does this show?
options: Continued army influence over elected governments
quiz.explain: Even under civilian rule, the army keeps strong influence.
steps: The case: an elected government holds office but generals shape defence and foreign policy.
Fact: since 2008 civilians rule, but the army keeps great influence.
So it shows continued army influence over elected governments.
Answer: Continued army influence over elected governments
quiz.mistake: Assumes elections alone remove military influence

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does Pakistan keep switching between generals and elected leaders?'
teach.praise: Hoot! The army, clergy and landlords are powerful, tensions with India help the army, and the Cold War backing hurt democracy too!
teach.nudge: You named the generals. But WHY was democracy weak there?

revise.summary: Pakistan swung between military and civilian rule: Ayub Khan (1958), Yahya Khan (1969), Bhutto (1971–77), Zia (1977), Benazir Bhutto (1988), Musharraf (1999), civilians since 2008. Democracy stayed weak due to dominant elites, conflict with India and Cold War outside support.
focus: Reasons democracy did not take root
remember: Ayub 1958 → Zia 1977 → Benazir 1988 → Musharraf 1999
Military, clergy and landowning aristocracy dominate society
The army keeps great influence even under elected governments
traps: Zia, not Yahya Khan, removed Bhutto in 1977.
Benazir Bhutto (1988) came before Nawaz Sharif.
Elections alone have not removed military influence.

topics.title: Democracy in Bangladesh

learn.hook: In 1971 a people won a war to protect their language and their vote. Building a stable democracy afterwards proved just as hard as winning freedom.
points: From 1947 to 1971, Bangladesh was East Pakistan. Its people resented domination by West Pakistan and the imposition of Urdu. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman of the Awami League led the struggle for autonomy.

In the 1970 elections, the Awami League won almost all the seats in East Pakistan (160 of 162), giving it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly. The West Pakistan leadership refused to accept this, and the army under General Yahya Khan cracked down and arrested Sheikh Mujib.
Millions fled to India as refugees. India supported the freedom struggle, and after war in December 1971, Bangladesh became independent.

Bangladesh's constitution declared it secular, democratic and socialist. In 1975 Sheikh Mujib changed it to a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League; he was assassinated that year in a military uprising.

Military-led rule followed (Ziaur Rahman, then H.M. Ershad). A mass protest movement forced Ershad to step down in 1990, and since 1991 Bangladesh has had a representative democracy with multi-party elections.

example.q: Order: Ershad steps down; Bangladesh becomes independent; Awami League wins 1970 elections; Sheikh Mujib assassinated.
steps: 1970: Awami League sweeps elections in East Pakistan.
1971: independence after war.
1975: Sheikh Mujib assassinated.
1990: Ershad steps down after mass protests.

learn.reallife: Bangladesh's garment factories now dress the world, and India and Bangladesh share rail, road and power links. The two countries share a history from 1971.

items.text: Before 1971, Bangladesh was known as East ___.
Sheikh Mujibur Rahman led the ___ League.
After Sheikh Mujib, military-led governments included those of Ziaur Rahman and H.M. ___.
Since ___, Bangladesh has had multi-party elections.

quiz.q: Before 1971, Bangladesh was known as:
quiz.explain: It was the eastern wing of Pakistan from 1947 to 1971.
steps: Fact: from 1947 to 1971 Bangladesh was East Pakistan.
West Bengal is an Indian state; Burma is Myanmar.
So East Pakistan.
Answer: East Pakistan
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the Indian state of West Bengal

quiz.q: Who led the Awami League in the struggle for Bangladesh?
quiz.explain: Sheikh Mujib led the Awami League and the freedom movement.
steps: Fact: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman of the Awami League led the struggle for autonomy.
Bhutto was a West Pakistan leader; Ershad and Ziaur Rahman came later.
So Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
Answer: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman

quiz.q: In the 1970 elections, the Awami League:
options: Won almost all seats in East Pakistan
quiz.explain: Its sweep gave it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly.
steps: Fact: in 1970 the Awami League won 160 of 162 seats in East Pakistan.
That gave it a majority in the proposed Constituent Assembly.
So it won almost all seats in East Pakistan.
Answer: Won almost all seats in East Pakistan

quiz.q: Which change did Sheikh Mujib make to the constitution in 1975?
options: He introduced a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League
quiz.explain: These changes concentrated power before his assassination later in 1975.
steps: Fact: in 1975 Sheikh Mujib changed the constitution.
He made it presidential and abolished all parties except the Awami League.
So he introduced a presidential system and banned other parties.
Answer: He introduced a presidential system and abolished all parties except the Awami League

quiz.q: Bangladesh has had representative democracy based on multi-party elections since:
quiz.explain: After Ershad stepped down in 1990, elections in 1991 restored democracy.
steps: Fact: mass protests forced Ershad out in 1990.
Since 1991 Bangladesh has had multi-party representative democracy.
1971 is independence, not the restoration of democracy.
Answer: 1991
quiz.mistake: Confuses independence with the restoration of democracy

quiz.q: India's role in 1971 was to:
options: Support the freedom struggle of the people of East Pakistan
quiz.explain: India backed the struggle, and the December 1971 war led to Bangladesh's independence.
steps: Fact: millions of refugees fled to India, and India supported the freedom struggle.
After the December 1971 war, Bangladesh became independent.
India did not annex the region; it supported the freedom struggle.
Answer: Support the freedom struggle of the people of East Pakistan

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The people of East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination. Reason (R): Urdu was imposed on them, and their elected majority was not honoured.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; R explains the resentment.
steps: A: true — East Pakistanis resented West Pakistan's domination.
R: true — Urdu was imposed and their electoral majority was denied.
R explains A: these were the causes of resentment.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Overlooks language and denial of electoral victory

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Bangladesh has never had military-led rule. Reason (R): The constitution of Bangladesh originally declared it secular, democratic and socialist.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: Ziaur Rahman and Ershad led military-backed rule. R is true.
steps: A: false — Ziaur Rahman and Ershad led military-led rule after 1975.
R: true — the original constitution was secular, democratic and socialist.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How was Bangladesh born, and has it always been a democracy?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971 under Sheikh Mujib, went through military rule, and has had multi-party democracy since 1991!
teach.nudge: You told me how it was born. What happened to democracy after 1975?

revise.summary: East Pakistan resented West Pakistan's domination and Urdu imposition. The Awami League under Sheikh Mujib swept the 1970 polls and, with India's support, Bangladesh became free in 1971. Military-led rule followed 1975; multi-party democracy since 1991.
focus: Causes of the Bangladesh freedom struggle
remember: Awami League won 160 of 162 East Pakistan seats in 1970
1975: presidential system, one party; Mujib assassinated
Ershad stepped down 1990; democracy since 1991
traps: Bangladesh did have military-led rule (Ziaur Rahman, Ershad).
Don't confuse independence (1971) with democracy restored (1991).
India supported the struggle; it did not annex the region.

topics.title: Monarchy and democracy in Nepal

learn.hook: In 2008 a country with one of the world's oldest ruling dynasties voted to abolish its monarchy. Nepal's path from king to republic took decades of protest.
points: Nepal was a Hindu kingdom in the past, and then a constitutional monarchy for many years in the modern period.
A strong pro-democracy movement in 1990 forced the king to accept a new democratic constitution. Democratic governments that followed were short-lived and troubled.
In the 1990s the Maoists, who opposed the monarchy and the ruling elite, built an armed insurgency in many parts of Nepal. In 2002 the king abolished the parliament and dismissed the government.
In April 2006 massive, country-wide pro-democracy protests by the Seven-Party Alliance (SPA), the Maoists and social activists forced the king to restore the House of Representatives.
In 2008 Nepal abolished the monarchy and became a democratic republic. A new Constitution was adopted in 2015.

example.q: Order these milestones in Nepal: monarchy abolished; king accepts democratic constitution after protests; new Constitution adopted; king restores parliament after mass protests.
steps: 1990: king accepts a democratic constitution.
2006: king restores the House of Representatives.
2008: monarchy abolished.
2015: new Constitution.

learn.reallife: India and Nepal share an open border; millions of Nepali citizens work in India and many have served in the Indian Army's Gorkha regiments, so Nepal's political changes are followed closely in India.

games.title: True or false?
items: The Maoists supported the absolute power of the king.
They opposed the monarchy and the ruling elite.
Nepal's new Constitution was adopted in 2015.
It came after the long constitution-making process.
The 2006 protests were led by the army.
They were led by the Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists.
In 1990 the king accepted a new democratic constitution.
A strong pro-democracy movement forced this.

quiz.q: Nepal abolished its monarchy and became a democratic republic in:
quiz.explain: The monarchy ended in 2008; the new Constitution came in 2015.
steps: Order: 1990 constitution, 2006 parliament restored, then monarchy ends, 2015 Constitution.
Fact: Nepal abolished the monarchy and became a republic in 2008.
2015 is the new Constitution, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 2008
quiz.mistake: Confuses the end of monarchy with the new Constitution

quiz.q: Which group led an armed insurgency against the monarchy in Nepal from the 1990s?
quiz.explain: The Maoists fought against the monarchy and the ruling elite.
steps: Fact: from the 1990s the Maoists built an armed insurgency in Nepal.
The Awami League is Bangladeshi, the LTTE Sri Lankan, the Taliban Afghan.
So the Maoists.
Answer: The Maoists
quiz.mistake: Picks a group from another South Asian country

quiz.q: The April 2006 pro-democracy movement in Nepal forced the king to:
quiz.explain: The king restored the parliament he had dissolved.
steps: Fact: the April 2006 country-wide protests forced the king to restore the House of Representatives.
The monarchy itself ended only in 2008.
So restore the House of Representatives.
Answer: Restore the House of Representatives
quiz.mistake: Thinks the 2006 movement immediately abolished the monarchy

quiz.q: Nepal's new Constitution was adopted in:
quiz.explain: After the monarchy was abolished, a new Constitution came in 2015.
steps: Fact: after the monarchy ended in 2008, a new Constitution was adopted in 2015.
2008 is the republic, not the Constitution.
Answer: 2015
quiz.mistake: Assumes the Constitution came the same year as the republic

quiz.q: What did the 1990 pro-democracy movement in Nepal achieve?
options: The king accepted a new democratic constitution
quiz.explain: The 1990 movement brought a democratic constitution while the monarchy continued.
steps: Fact: in 1990 a pro-democracy movement forced the king to accept a new democratic constitution.
The monarchy continued until 2008.
So the king accepted a new democratic constitution.
Answer: The king accepted a new democratic constitution

quiz.q: Who were part of the 2006 movement for democracy in Nepal?
options: The Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists
quiz.explain: A broad coalition joined the protests.
steps: Fact: the 2006 protests were led by the Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists.
It was a broad coalition, not the royal army or foreign governments.
So the SPA, the Maoists and social activists.
Answer: The Seven-Party Alliance, the Maoists and social activists
quiz.mistake: Thinks one group alone led the movement

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Nepal is now a democratic republic. Reason (R): Its monarchy was abolished in 2008.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the abolition of the monarchy made Nepal a republic.
steps: A: true — Nepal is now a democratic republic.
R: true — its monarchy was abolished in 2008.
R explains A: ending the monarchy made Nepal a republic.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect abolition of monarchy with republic status

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Democracy in Nepal was fully stable after 1990. Reason (R): The Maoist insurgency spread in many parts of Nepal in the 1990s.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the 1990s were turbulent. R is true.
steps: A: false — governments after 1990 were short-lived and troubled.
R: true — the Maoist insurgency spread in the 1990s.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Assumes one constitution solved all problems

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Nepal had a king? What happened to him, and when?'
teach.praise: Wow! A king, protests in 1990 and 2006, the Maoist insurgency, and finally a republic in 2008 with a Constitution in 2015!
teach.nudge: When exactly did Nepal stop having a king? And who pushed for it?

revise.summary: Nepal moved from monarchy towards democracy: a 1990 democratic constitution, a Maoist insurgency, the king dissolving parliament in 2002, the 2006 movement restoring it, the monarchy abolished in 2008 and a new Constitution in 2015.
focus: Role of the Maoists and the 2006 movement
remember: 1990 democratic constitution; 2006 House restored
2008 monarchy abolished, republic formed
2015 new Constitution
traps: Don't confuse 2008 (republic) with 2015 (Constitution).
The 2006 movement restored parliament; it did not itself end the monarchy.
Democracy after 1990 was not stable.

topics.title: Ethnic conflict and democracy in Sri Lanka

learn.hook: Sri Lanka has kept holding elections since 1948, yet for over two decades it also fought one of Asia's longest civil wars.
points: Sri Lanka has remained a democracy since independence in 1948, but faced a serious ethnic conflict. Sinhala nationalists believed Sri Lanka should belong to the Sinhala majority and resisted concessions to the Tamil minority.

Neglect of Tamil concerns led to militant Tamil nationalism. From 1983 the LTTE (Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam) fought an armed struggle against the army, demanding 'Tamil Eelam', a separate country for Sri Lankan Tamils.

In 1987 India signed an accord with Sri Lanka and sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to help stabilise the situation. The IPKF got into fighting with the LTTE, and the move was unpopular among many Sri Lankans and Tamils in India. The IPKF was withdrawn without achieving its aim.
The conflict ended in 2009 when the LTTE was defeated by the Sri Lankan army.

Despite the conflict, Sri Lanka recorded considerable economic growth and high levels of human development. It was one of the first developing countries to control population growth and the first in the region to liberalise its economy.

example.q: Explain why the LTTE demanded Tamil Eelam.
steps: Sinhala majority nationalism dominated politics after 1948.
Tamil concerns were neglected, causing alienation.
Militant Tamil groups, led by the LTTE from 1983, demanded a separate country, Tamil Eelam.
example.answer: Because of Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of Tamil concerns

learn.reallife: Tamil Nadu and northern Sri Lanka are separated only by the narrow Palk Strait, which is why events in Sri Lanka have always drawn strong interest in Indian politics.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Separate country demanded by the LTTE

quiz.explain: The LTTE fought for Tamil Eelam.
steps: The LTTE fought for 'Tamil Eelam', a separate Tamil country.
Its full name is Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.
The other expansions are made up.
Answer: Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam

quiz.q: India sent the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) to Sri Lanka in:
quiz.explain: India signed an accord and sent the IPKF in 1987.

Answer: It achieved high levels of human development despite the conflict

quiz.mistake: Thinks the IPKF supported the LTTE

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

teach.nudge: Good start. What did the LTTE want, and how did India get involved?

revise.summary: Sri Lanka stayed democratic since 1948 but Sinhala majoritarianism and neglect of Tamils led to the LTTE's armed struggle for Tamil Eelam from 1983. India's IPKF (1987) was unpopular and withdrawn; the LTTE was defeated in 2009. Sri Lanka still achieved high human development.

IPKF sent in 1987; LTTE defeated in 2009

topics.title: India-Pakistan conflicts

learn.hook: Two countries born on the same night in 1947 have fought several wars, share rivers, and in 1998 both declared themselves nuclear powers.
points: Kashmir has been the core issue between India and Pakistan since Partition. They fought wars in 1947-48 and 1965. In 1971 war broke out over East Pakistan, leading to Bangladesh. In 1999 they fought the Kargil conflict.
Other disputes include control of the Siachen glacier and the boundary line in Sir Creek, a strip of water in the Rann of Kutch.
River waters: the Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960, with the World Bank's mediation, to share the waters of the Indus river system.
Both countries tested nuclear devices in 1998 (India in May, Pakistan soon after). This intensified an arms race between them.
India has accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism and militant groups, while the two sides have also tried confidence-building measures and dialogue at times.

example.q: List three non-Kashmir disputes between India and Pakistan.
steps: Siachen glacier.
Sir Creek in the Rann of Kutch.
Sharing of river waters (Indus system).
example.answer: Siachen, Sir Creek, river waters

learn.reallife: Farmers in Punjab depend on the Indus river system, which is why the 1960 water treaty matters as much to agriculture as to diplomacy.

quiz.explain: The World Bank brokered the treaty.

Answer: 1999

Answer: 1998

So Kashmir.
Answer: Kashmir

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The arms race between India and Pakistan intensified after 1998. Reason (R): Both countries conducted nuclear tests in 1998.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and the tests explain the sharper arms race.
steps: A: true — the arms race intensified after 1998.

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link nuclear tests with the arms race

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why do India and Pakistan keep quarrelling? Is it only about Kashmir?'
teach.praise: Got it! Kashmir is the core, with wars in 1947-48, 1965, 1971 and Kargil, plus Siachen, Sir Creek, rivers and nuclear rivalry!
teach.nudge: You said Kashmir. What other disputes are there?

revise.summary: Kashmir is the core India–Pakistan issue, with wars in 1947–48, 1965, 1971 and Kargil in 1999. Other disputes are Siachen, Sir Creek and river waters (Indus Waters Treaty 1960, World Bank). Both tested nuclear devices in 1998.
focus: Wars and disputes between India and Pakistan
remember: Indus Waters Treaty: 1960, mediated by the World Bank
Sir Creek: boundary in the Rann of Kutch; Siachen: glacier
Nuclear tests 1998; Kargil 1999
traps: Don't confuse Kargil (1999) with the nuclear tests (1998).
Sir Creek is not the Siachen glacier.

topics.title: India and its other neighbours

learn.hook: When a coup attempt shook the Maldives in 1988, Indian paratroopers arrived within hours. India's ties with its smaller neighbours mix help, friction and deep connections.
points: India-Bangladesh: differences over sharing the waters of the Ganga and Brahmaputra, illegal migration into India and border management. They also cooperate on trade, energy, disaster management and connectivity, and Bangladesh is part of India's Look East policy.

India-Nepal: a treaty allows citizens of both countries to travel and work in each other's country without visas and passports. Friction has arisen over Nepal's ties with China, trade and the Maoist movement, yet economic, scientific and cultural ties remain strong.
India-Sri Lanka: the Tamil issue and the IPKF strained ties, but relations have improved. A free trade agreement was signed, and India helped Sri Lanka after the 2004 tsunami.
India-Bhutan: a very close relationship. India supports hydroelectric projects in Bhutan, and Bhutan's king helped flush out guerrillas from north-eastern India operating from Bhutanese territory.
India-Maldives: in 1988, when mercenaries attacked the Maldives, India's air force and navy responded quickly at the Maldives' request (Operation Cactus).

example.q: Which neighbour fits each clue: (a) open border, no visa needed (b) hydroelectric partner (c) Operation Cactus (1988)?
steps: (a) Nepal: open border by treaty.
(b) Bhutan: India supports hydro projects.
(c) Maldives: India foiled the 1988 coup attempt.
example.answer: Nepal, Bhutan, Maldives

learn.reallife: Electricity from Bhutan's hydro plants lights homes in eastern India, and Nepali workers are a familiar part of many Indian cities.

Answer: Sharing of Ganga and Brahmaputra waters

Answer: Cooperation on disaster management alongside disputes

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Besides Pakistan, how does India get along with its other neighbours?'

topics.title: SAARC, SAFTA and outside powers

learn.hook: South Asia is home to a huge share of the world's people, yet trade among its countries remains small. SAARC was meant to change that.
points: The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was set up in 1985 by the South Asian states to cooperate by peaceful means. Afghanistan later joined, and its secretariat is in Kathmandu.
Members signed the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) agreement in 2004, aiming to lower trade barriers across the region. It came into effect in 2006.
Some neighbours feared SAFTA would let India dominate their markets, while India's small neighbours also saw benefits from its large market.
SAARC's progress has been limited mainly by India-Pakistan tensions and political differences among members.

Outside powers matter in South Asia: China has close strategic ties with Pakistan and growing links with other neighbours, and the USA has become an important player, keeping good relations with both India and Pakistan. Comparing democracy across states and evaluating SAARC are common exercise themes.

example.q: Evaluate SAARC in two points: one achievement and one limitation.
steps: Achievement: SAFTA (2004) as a step towards regional free trade.
Limitation: progress held back by India-Pakistan tensions.
example.answer: SAFTA was achieved, but India-Pakistan tensions limit SAARC

learn.reallife: Students from all eight SAARC countries study at the South Asian University in New Delhi, set up by SAARC states, showing cooperation beyond trade.

topics.title: Why international organisations? The birth of the UN

learn.hook: Climate change, pandemics and wars do not stop at borders. Countries need a common table where they can talk before they fight. That table is the United Nations.
points: International organisations help countries cooperate on issues of war and peace and on shared problems such as disease, poverty and the environment. They are not a world government; they work through the cooperation of member states.
They provide rules, a forum for discussion and information, which make collective action easier and cheaper. They can also help resolve disputes before they become wars.
The League of Nations, set up after the First World War, failed to prevent the Second World War. The United Nations was founded in 1945 as its successor, and 51 states signed the UN Charter.
The UN's main aims are to prevent international conflict and to foster cooperation among states for social and economic development.
The UN has 193 member states today, making it the most important international organisation.

example.q: Why did the world create the UN in 1945 when the League of Nations already existed?
steps: The League had failed to prevent the Second World War.
The war's destruction convinced states they needed a stronger body.
So the UN was set up in 1945 as the League's successor, to prevent conflict and promote cooperation.
example.answer: Because the League of Nations had failed to prevent the Second World War

learn.reallife: Indian Army peacekeepers serve under the blue UN flag in Africa and the Middle East, a direct example of countries working together through an international organisation.

topics.title: Principal organs of the UN and the Security Council

learn.hook: Five countries can stop any big UN decision with a single word: 'No'. That word is the veto, and it sits at the heart of the Security Council.
points: The UN has six principal organs: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council.

The General Assembly includes all members, each with one vote. ECOSOC deals with economic and social issues. The International Court of Justice at The Hague settles legal disputes between states. The Trusteeship Council has suspended its operations.

The Security Council is responsible for international peace and security. It has 15 members: 5 permanent members (USA, Russia, UK, France, China) and 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.
The permanent members (P5) have the veto: a negative vote by any one of them blocks a substantive decision, even if all others agree. Non-permanent members do not have the veto.

example.q: A resolution in the Security Council gets 14 'yes' votes and 1 'no' vote from France. Does it pass?
steps: France is a permanent member.
A 'no' from a permanent member is a veto.
A veto blocks a substantive resolution regardless of other votes.
example.answer: No. France's negative vote is a veto

learn.reallife: India has served many terms as a non-permanent member of the Security Council, most recently in 2021-22, but has no veto, which is why it campaigns for a permanent seat.

topics.title: The Secretary-General and UN agencies

learn.hook: Childhood vaccines, refugee camps, heritage sites like the Taj Mahal: the UN family touches daily life in ways most people never notice.
points: The Secretary-General heads the Secretariat and is the chief administrative officer and representative of the UN. The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation.

Secretaries-General in order: Trygve Lie (Norway), Dag Hammarskjöld (Sweden), U Thant (Burma, now Myanmar), Kurt Waldheim (Austria), Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (Peru), Boutros Boutros-Ghali (Egypt), Kofi Annan (Ghana), Ban Ki-moon (South Korea), António Guterres (Portugal, from 2017).
WHO (World Health Organisation) works for good health for all. UNDP (UN Development Programme) supports development. UNICEF (UN Children's Fund) protects children's rights and welfare.

UNESCO (UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) works on education, science and culture, including World Heritage Sites. UNHCR (UN High Commissioner for Refugees) protects refugees. UNHRC (UN Human Rights Council) monitors human rights.

example.q: A town in India hosts a polio vaccination drive, and a nearby fort is named a World Heritage Site. Which UN agencies are involved?
steps: Health and vaccination: WHO (with UNICEF supporting child immunisation).
World Heritage Sites: UNESCO.
example.answer: WHO (and UNICEF) for vaccines; UNESCO for heritage

learn.reallife: India's victory over polio, declared in 2014, was achieved with support from WHO and UNICEF. Many Indian monuments, from Hampi to the Sundarbans, are on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

topics.title: Why reform the UN? Expanding the Security Council

learn.hook: The Security Council's permanent members were fixed in 1945, when many of today's members were still colonies. Should a council designed for 1945 still run the world?
points: After the Cold War, calls for reform grew: membership had risen from 51 to 193, the world had become unipolar, and new challenges such as terrorism, civil wars and climate change had emerged.

Reform has two parts: reform of the organisation's structures and processes, and a review of the issues within its jurisdiction. Most agree the Security Council's structure should change, especially by adding members.

In 1992 the General Assembly adopted a resolution reflecting complaints that the Security Council no longer represented contemporary political realities, that its decisions reflected only Western values and interests, and that it lacked equitable representation.

Criteria proposed for new permanent members include being a major economic power, a major military power, a substantial contributor to the UN budget, a big nation in terms of population, a nation that respects democracy and human rights, and a country that would make the Council more representative in geography, economic systems and culture.
Each criterion is debated: for example, how big an economy or how large a population is 'enough'. The future of the veto is also debated.

example.q: A country has a large population and respects democracy but is not a major military power. Can it fully meet the proposed criteria?
steps: Criteria include economy, military, budget contribution, population, democracy and representativeness.
It meets population and democracy.
It does not meet the military criterion, so it meets only some criteria; each one is debated.
example.answer: Only partly; it meets some criteria but not all

learn.reallife: Debates on Security Council reform often feature India, Brazil, Germany and Japan, the 'G4' who support each other's claims to permanent seats.

topics.title: Reforming the UN's jurisdiction: the 2005 decisions

learn.hook: In 2005, at its 60th birthday, the UN made a list of promises. Some created new bodies that still work today.
points: Jurisdiction reform asks which issues the UN should deal with: peace and security (including peacekeeping), terrorism, human rights, climate change, poverty and development.
In September 2005, world leaders met to mark the UN's 60th anniversary and agreed on steps to make the UN more relevant.

Decisions included creating a Peacebuilding Commission, accepting the international community's responsibility to protect people if national governments fail to protect their own citizens from atrocities, and creating a Human Rights Council (operational since 2006).
They also agreed to achieve the Millennium Development Goals, condemned terrorism in all its forms, created a Democracy Fund, and agreed to wind up the Trusteeship Council.
Disagreements remain over issues such as the definition of terrorism and how to act when states fail to protect citizens.

example.q: Which 2005 decision deals with helping countries recover after conflict?
steps: The Peacebuilding Commission was created to plan and support recovery in post-conflict societies.
The Human Rights Council deals with human rights; the Democracy Fund supports democracy.

topics.title: India and UN reforms

learn.hook: India sent peacekeepers to Korea, Congo, Lebanon and beyond, yet has no permanent seat at the UN's top table. Here is the case India makes, and the objections it faces.
points: India supports restructuring the UN to make it more democratic and effective, including enlarging the Security Council to make it more representative.

India's case for permanent membership: it is one of the world's most populous countries and the largest democracy; it has taken part in almost all UN initiatives; it has a long, substantial record in UN peacekeeping; its economy is among the largest; and it pays its UN dues regularly.

Objections and debates: some question India's nuclear weapons capability; some think rivalry with Pakistan would make India less effective; some argue other regions (such as Africa and South America) should be represented; and some oppose expanding the veto.
India's view: it should get a permanent seat with the same powers as current members.

example.q: Build India's case in three points for a board answer.

steps: Fact: some argue other regions, such as Africa and South America, should be represented.
This is the regional-representation argument.
So regions like Africa and South America also need permanent seats.

quiz.q: What does India say about the powers a new permanent member should have?

The same powers as existing permanent members

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India has a strong claim to a permanent seat. Reason (R): India has taken part in almost all UN initiatives and in many peacekeeping missions.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; its UN record supports its claim.
steps: A: true — India has a strong claim to a permanent seat.
R: true — it has joined almost all UN initiatives and many peacekeeping missions.
R explains A: this record supports the claim.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: there are objections. R is true and is one such objection.
steps: A: false — there are objections, so not every member supports India.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why should India get a permanent seat? And why doesn't everyone agree?'
teach.praise: Hooray! India is a huge democracy, a big peacekeeper and a large economy, but some raise its nuclear status, the Pakistan rivalry and other regions' claims.
teach.nudge: You made India's case. What objections do others raise?

topics.title: The UN in a unipolar world

learn.hook: The UN's headquarters is in New York, and one country pays the largest share of its budget. Can the UN still check that country's power?
points: After the Cold War, the USA's power grew and it faced few checks. Many hoped the UN could balance US dominance, but this is difficult.
The USA is the single largest contributor to the UN budget, the UN is physically located in the USA, and Americans hold many important positions in its bureaucracy.
The USA has a veto in the Security Council, so it can block moves against its interests. It also has great influence over the choice of the Secretary-General.

Despite these limits, the UN remains an important forum: it lets states discuss and criticise policies (including US policies), share concerns and seek compromise. Without it, the world would be worse off.

example.q: Give two reasons why the UN finds it hard to check US power.
steps: The USA is the largest contributor to the UN budget.
It holds a veto in the Security Council and can block decisions.
example.answer: Largest budget contributor; holds the veto

learn.reallife: Indian diplomats use UN debates to raise issues such as terrorism and climate justice even when big powers disagree, showing how the UN works as a forum for all.

games.title: Source of US influence or role of the UN as a forum?
buckets: Source of US influence in the UN
UN as a forum for all

States can criticise big powers in debates

Answer: It is the single largest contributor to the UN budget

steps: Fact: the USA is a permanent member of the Security Council.

Answer: It has a veto as a permanent member

quiz.q: Despite US dominance, the UN is useful because:
options: It can order the USA to change its government

quiz.explain: The UN provides an arena for dialogue.
steps: The UN cannot order the USA to change, tax its citizens or outgun it.

So it is useful as a forum for dialogue.
Answer: It is a forum where states can discuss, criticise and seek compromise

quiz.q: Who has great influence over the choice of the UN Secretary-General?
options: The USA, among the permanent members
quiz.explain: The P5, especially the USA, strongly influence the choice.
steps: Fact: the USA has great influence over the choice of the Secretary-General.
This comes from its position among the veto-holding permanent members.
So the USA, among the permanent members.
Answer: The USA, among the permanent members
quiz.mistake: Ignores the role of the veto powers

quiz.q: In a unipolar world, the UN's ability to balance the dominant power is:
options: Greater than during the Cold War
Equal to that of the superpower
quiz.explain: The UN depends on the support of its strongest members.
steps: Many hoped the UN could balance US dominance.
Fact: this is difficult because of US funding, location and veto.
So the UN's ability is limited.
Answer: Limited

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The UN cannot easily balance US dominance. Reason (R): The USA has a veto and is the largest contributor to the UN budget.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the veto and funding explain the limit.
steps: A: true — the UN cannot easily balance US dominance.
R: true — the USA has a veto and is the largest budget contributor.
R explains A: these give the USA its weight in the UN.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to connect US resources with UN limits

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The UN has no value in a unipolar world. Reason (R): The UN offers states an arena to discuss and criticise even powerful countries' policies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: the UN remains valuable. R is true and shows why.
steps: A: false — the UN remains an important forum.
R: true — it lets states discuss and criticise even powerful countries.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If America is so strong, what's the point of the UN?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The US funds the UN most and has a veto, so the UN can't easily check it, but it's still a forum where everyone can talk!
teach.nudge: Good. Why is it hard for the UN to balance US power? Think of money and votes.

revise.summary: In a unipolar world the UN finds it hard to check the USA, which is the largest budget contributor, hosts the UN in New York, holds key posts and has a veto. Still, the UN remains a valuable forum for dialogue and criticism.

topics.title: IMF, World Bank and WTO

learn.hook: In 1991 India faced a severe balance of payments crisis and turned to the IMF for help. These institutions shape the economic choices of nations.
points: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) oversees financial institutions and regulations that act at the international level. Voting is not equal: each country's vote is weighted by how much it has contributed, and the richest countries, led by the USA, hold the largest shares.

The World Bank was created in 1944 and works for development: human development (education, health), agriculture and rural development, environmental protection, infrastructure (roads, electricity) and governance. It gives loans and grants to member countries.
The World Bank is criticised for setting the economic agenda of poorer countries, attaching strict conditions to its loans and pushing free market reforms.
The World Trade Organisation (WTO), set up in 1995 as the successor to GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, created after the Second World War), sets the rules for global trade.
WTO decisions are taken by consensus, but the major economic powers such as the USA, the EU and Japan have dominated its rule-making. Developing countries often complain that the rules are not fair.

example.q: Match each need to an institution: (a) a loan to build rural roads (b) a dispute over import duties (c) help to manage a currency crisis.
steps: (a) Development project: World Bank.
(b) Trade rules and disputes: WTO.
(c) International financial stability: IMF.
example.answer: World Bank, WTO, IMF

learn.reallife: Indian farmers' groups and the government regularly debate WTO rules on farm subsidies, because these rules affect minimum support prices and food security programmes.

items.text: The WTO was set up in ___.

Answer: 1995
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with GATT or China's entry (2001)

quiz.explain: GATT was created after the Second World War and was replaced by the WTO.

Answer: GATT

steps: Fact: the World Bank is criticised for setting poor countries' agendas.

Answer: Agriculture and rural development

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Rich countries have the greatest say in the IMF. Reason (R): IMF votes are weighted according to each country's financial contribution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

steps: A: true — rich countries have the greatest say in the IMF.

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see how weighted voting works

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The World Bank was created in 1995. Reason (R): The World Bank gives loans and grants for development.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'IMF, World Bank, WTO... what does each one actually do?'

teach.nudge: Good. Which one sets trade rules, and which one gives development loans?

revise.summary: The IMF oversees international finance with votes weighted by contribution, so rich countries dominate. The World Bank (1944) funds development but is criticised for loan conditions. The WTO (1995), successor to GATT, sets trade rules dominated by major powers.

topics.title: IAEA, ILO, NGOs and the future of international organisations

learn.hook: Inspectors with radiation meters, labour experts in Geneva, volunteers documenting abuses: international cooperation goes far beyond politicians giving speeches.
points: The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), set up in 1957, grew out of US President Eisenhower's 'Atoms for Peace' proposal. It promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and works to prevent its military use; its inspectors regularly visit nuclear facilities.

The International Labour Organisation (ILO), founded in 1919 and later a UN specialised agency, sets international labour standards and promotes workers' rights. Governments, employers and workers are all represented in it.

Amnesty International is an NGO that campaigns for the protection of human rights all over the world and publishes reports on violations. Human Rights Watch is an international NGO that does research and advocacy on human rights and draws media attention to abuses.
NGOs are not set up by governments, but they influence states and international organisations by gathering information and mobilising public opinion.

The future: international organisations are imperfect but essential. They need reform to stay relevant, and countries like India seek a bigger voice in them. Common exercises ask you to match organisations with their functions and argue for or against Security Council reform.

example.q: Match the body to the clue: (a) inspects nuclear plants (b) labour standards (c) human rights campaigns by a non-governmental group.
steps: (a) IAEA: nuclear inspections.
(b) ILO: labour standards and workers' rights.
(c) Amnesty International or Human Rights Watch: NGOs on human rights.
example.answer: IAEA, ILO, Amnesty International / Human Rights Watch

learn.reallife: India's civil nuclear plants, such as Kudankulam, operate under IAEA safeguards, and Indian labour laws are often discussed against ILO standards.
