topics.title: Linguistic states: from Potti Sriramulu to the SRC

learn.hook: In 1952 a veteran Gandhian refused food for 56 days, demanding a state for Telugu speakers. His death changed India's map.
points: During the national movement, the Congress, at its Nagpur session in 1920, recognised the linguistic principle and reorganised its own provincial committees by language.
After independence, national leaders hesitated, fearing that division on linguistic lines, so soon after Partition, might threaten unity.

The Vishalandhra movement demanded a separate state for Telugu speakers. Potti Sriramulu, a Congress leader and veteran Gandhian, went on an indefinite fast and died after 56 days, sparking widespread protests.
The Prime Minister then announced the formation of a separate Andhra state in December 1952, and Andhra state came into being in 1953.

The central government appointed the States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) in 1953. It accepted that state boundaries should reflect the boundaries of different languages. The States Reorganisation Act was passed in 1956, creating 14 states and 6 union territories.

topics.title: Later reorganisations and the lesson of linguistic states

learn.hook: India's map has kept changing, from two new states in 1960 to Telangana in 2014. Each change shows democracy accommodating diversity.
points: In 1960 the bilingual Bombay state was divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat. In 1966 Punjab was reorganised, and Haryana was created (with hill areas going to Himachal Pradesh).
In the North-East, Nagaland became a state in 1963, and Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura became states in 1972. Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh followed in 1987.
In 2000, three new states were created: Chhattisgarh (from Madhya Pradesh), Uttarakhand (from Uttar Pradesh) and Jharkhand (from Bihar). Telangana was carved out of Andhra Pradesh in 2014.

Linguistic states turned out to strengthen national unity: by recognising diversity, India accommodated regional demands democratically instead of suppressing them. The fear that they would break India proved wrong.

chapters.title: Politics in India: Era of One-Party Dominance

topics.title: The challenge of building democracy: the first general election

learn.hook: In 1951-52 about 17 crore Indians, most of whom could not read, were invited to choose their government. Many observers abroad expected the experiment to fail. It did not.
points: India chose democracy with universal adult franchise from the start: every adult citizen got the right to vote, regardless of literacy, wealth, caste or gender. Many countries had given this right only gradually.
The Election Commission of India was set up in January 1950, and Sukumar Sen became the first Chief Election Commissioner.

The first general election was a huge exercise: about 17 crore voters, most of them not literate, electing about 489 members of the Lok Sabha and members of state assemblies. It was postponed twice and finally held from October 1951 to February 1952.

Voting methods have changed: in the first two elections each candidate had a separate ballot box marked with a symbol, and voters dropped their ballot paper into the box of their choice. Later, ballot papers listed names and symbols, and from the late 1990s Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) were introduced; by 2004 the whole country used EVMs.
The success of the first election proved that democracy could work even in a poor and largely non-literate country.

learn.reallife: Today's EVMs and VVPATs, used in elections from Ladakh to Lakshadweep, grew out of the Election Commission's long effort to make voting simpler and faster.

topics.title: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

learn.hook: In 1952 one party won about three out of every four seats in the Lok Sabha, yet less than half the votes. The secret lies in the voting system.
points: The Congress won the first three general elections (1952, 1957 and 1962) by large margins and also formed governments in almost all states.
In 1952 the Congress won 364 of the 489 Lok Sabha seats. The Communist Party of India came second with only 16 seats.

India uses the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority. Because opposition votes were split among many parties, the Congress won about three-fourths of the seats with less than half of the votes.

An exception came in Kerala in 1957, where the Communist Party of India won the assembly election and formed a government under E.M.S. Namboodiripad. The central government dismissed it in 1959 under Article 356.

example.q: In a constituency, Congress gets 40% votes, Party B 35% and Party C 25%. Who wins under FPTP, and why does this matter?
steps: Under FPTP, the candidate with the most votes wins.
Congress has the most votes (40%), so it wins, even though 60% voted against it.
Repeated across many constituencies, this gives a seat share much bigger than the vote share.
example.answer: Congress wins; FPTP can turn a minority of votes into a large share of seats

learn.reallife: A batsman who scores the most runs wins 'man of the match' even if he did not score half the team's runs. FPTP rewards the top scorer in each seat the same way.

topics.title: Nature of Congress dominance: a social and ideological coalition

learn.hook: One party, many voices: socialists and conservatives, farmers and industrialists, villagers and city folk, all under one roof.
points: One-party dominance existed in other countries too, but often without democracy. For example, the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) ruled Mexico for about sixty years under conditions that were not fully democratic. In India, Congress dominance happened under free and fair, democratic elections.
Its roots lay in the legacy of the national movement: the Congress was seen as the inheritor of the freedom struggle, and it had the widest organisation, reaching almost every village.
The Congress was a social coalition: it brought together peasants and industrialists, urban and rural people, workers and owners, the middle, lower and upper classes and castes.
It was also an ideological coalition: it accommodated revolutionaries and pacifists, conservatives and radicals, extremists and moderates, and those on the right, left and centre.

example.q: How was Congress dominance in India different from the PRI's dominance in Mexico?
steps: The PRI ruled Mexico for decades under conditions that were not fully democratic.
The Congress won repeatedly in free and fair elections with many opposition parties.
So Indian one-party dominance existed within democracy.
example.answer: Congress dominance was achieved democratically; the PRI's was not

topics.title: Tolerance and management of factions

learn.hook: In the early years, some of the sharpest criticism of the Congress came from inside the Congress itself.
points: Groups within a party are called factions. The Congress had many factions based on ideology or personal ambition and rivalries.
Instead of being a weakness, factions became a strength: they acted as an internal opposition, criticising leaders and policies from within, and forcing the party to adjust.

The coalition-like nature of the Congress encouraged tolerance of differences. Even a faction that was unhappy with the leadership usually stayed inside the party and tried to change it, rather than leaving.
Because of this, the Congress could accommodate many interests, and opposition parties found it hard to grow, since many of their concerns were already voiced by groups within the Congress.

example.q: Why did unhappy groups often stay within the Congress rather than leave?
steps: The party tolerated differences and had a coalition character.

learn.reallife: In a cricket team, players may argue about batting order but still play for the same side. Congress factions behaved much the same way.

topics.title: Opposition parties: the Socialists and the Communists

learn.hook: Some of India's earliest opposition leaders had sat in Congress meetings for years before walking out to build their own parties.
points: The Congress Socialist Party was formed within the Congress in 1934 by young leaders who wanted a more radical, egalitarian Congress. In 1948 the Congress barred dual membership, so the socialists left and formed the Socialist Party.

Leaders of the socialists included Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan. They believed in democratic socialism and criticised the Congress for favouring capitalists and landlords. The party later went through many splits and mergers.
Communist groups emerged in the early 1920s, inspired by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia. The Communist Party of India (CPI) worked with the Congress for some years before separating.

CPI leaders included A.K. Gopalan, S.A. Dange, E.M.S. Namboodiripad, P.C. Joshi, Ajay Ghosh and P. Sundarraya. In 1952 the CPI won 16 seats and was the largest opposition party. It split in 1964, and the CPI(M) was formed.

topics.title: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party and the role of the opposition

learn.hook: Nehru's first cabinet included leaders who would later found or lead rival parties. Early Indian democracy valued a strong opposition voice.
points: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951, with Syama Prasad Mookerjee as its founder-president. It emphasised the idea of one country, one culture and one nation, believing the country could become modern and strong on the basis of Indian culture and traditions. It favoured Hindi as the official language. Leaders included Deen Dayal Upadhyaya and Balraj Madhok. It is the precursor of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

The Swatantra Party was formed in August 1959 after the Congress's Nagpur resolution called for land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming. Its leaders included C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, N.G. Ranga and Minoo Masani.
The Swatantra Party favoured a free-market economy and less government control. It opposed central planning, nationalisation and the licence system, and favoured closer ties with the USA.

Although they won few seats, opposition parties played a crucial role: they offered principled criticism of Congress policies, kept the ruling party accountable and prevented resentment from becoming anti-democratic.

Early leaders respected the opposition: Nehru's first cabinet after independence (before the first general election) included non-Congress figures like B.R. Ambedkar and Syama Prasad Mookerjee. Exercise tip: match parties with their leaders and explain Congress dominance.

example.q: Match each party with its founding leader: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party, Socialist Party.
steps: Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Syama Prasad Mookerjee (1951).
Swatantra Party: C. Rajagopalachari (1959).
Socialist Party: Acharya Narendra Dev, among others.
example.answer: BJS - Mookerjee; Swatantra - Rajagopalachari; Socialist - Narendra Dev

chapters.title: Politics in India: Politics of Planned Development

topics.title: Political contestations over development

learn.hook: A hill rich in iron ore can mean a steel plant and thousands of jobs, or forests lost and villages displaced. Which path should a state choose, and who decides?
points: Development decisions are political: they involve choices between different groups with competing interests, and so they are contested in a democracy.
No single decision suits everyone. What benefits one group, such as industry or urban consumers, may harm another, such as tribal communities or farmers.
Example: Odisha has some of the largest untapped reserves of iron ore in India. The state government signed agreements with steel companies to set up plants, hoping for investment and jobs.

Tribal communities feared displacement from their land and loss of livelihood; environmentalists warned of pollution and damage to forests; others argued that industry was essential for the state's growth.
Such debates show that the question of development is not just technical but also about values and whose interests count.

steps: State government and industry: want investment, jobs and growth.
Tribal communities: fear displacement and loss of livelihood.

example.answer: Government and industry; tribal communities; environmentalists

learn.reallife: Debates over new airports, expressways, dams or mines in your own state follow the same pattern: jobs and growth on one side, displacement and environment on the other.

topics.title: Ideas of development: which model?

learn.hook: In 1947 India had two famous models to copy: the American and the Soviet. It chose neither completely.
points: In the 1940s and 1950s, development was often understood as becoming 'modern', which meant becoming like the industrialised countries of the West. Modernisation was linked with growth, industrialisation and material progress.
There were two models of modern development: the liberal-capitalist model, as in the USA and much of Europe, and the socialist model, as in the USSR.
Many Indian leaders, including Nehru, were impressed by the Soviet model of rapid industrialisation, but India did not copy either model fully.

Left and right: the 'left' favoured pro-poor policies and a strong role for the state to reduce inequality; the 'right' favoured free competition and a market economy, with less government interference.
India's leaders agreed that development could not be left to private actors alone; the state had to play a key role. They disagreed about how much.

example.q: Classify these views as left or right: (a) the state should own key industries to reduce inequality (b) markets should decide prices with minimal government role.
steps: (a) Strong state role for the poor: left.
(b) Free market and less interference: right.
example.answer: (a) left; (b) right

learn.reallife: Debates today about privatising public sector banks or Air India are modern versions of the old left-right debate on the state's role.

topics.title: Planning: the Bombay Plan, the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog

learn.hook: Surprisingly, one of the strongest calls for state planning in India came from big industrialists, in 1944.
points: There was a broad consensus that India should plan its development. In 1944, a group of big industrialists drafted a joint proposal for a planned economy, called the Bombay Plan. It wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investments.

The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950 by a simple resolution of the Government of India. It had an advisory role, and the Prime Minister was its chairperson. It was not set up by the Constitution or by a separate law.

A Five Year Plan is a document in which the government sets out its plan for income and expenditure over five years. Planning lets the government focus on the larger picture and make long-term interventions in the economy.
The Planning Commission was replaced by the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) in 2015.

example.q: Was the Planning Commission a constitutional body?
steps: It was set up in March 1950.
It was created by a simple resolution of the Government of India.
So it was neither constitutional nor statutory; it was advisory.
example.answer: No; it was set up by a government resolution and was advisory

learn.reallife: NITI Aayog now publishes indices like the SDG India Index and works with states, instead of drawing up Five Year Plans.

topics.title: The First and Second Five Year Plans

learn.hook: The First Plan said: feed the nation first. The Second Plan said: build steel, power and machines fast. Two plans, two philosophies.
points: The First Five Year Plan (1951-56) focused on the agrarian sector, including investment in dams and irrigation. Agriculture had been badly hit by Partition, and land reforms were seen as key to development.
K.N. Raj, a young economist who helped draft the First Plan, argued that India should 'hasten slowly' for the first two decades.
The Second Five Year Plan (1956-61) stressed heavy industrialisation, and was drafted under the leadership of P.C. Mahalanobis.
To protect domestic industries, the government imposed substantial tariffs on imports. Public sector industries were set up in steel, power and machinery.
Exam tip: First Plan = agriculture, dams, irrigation, K.N. Raj; Second Plan = heavy industry, P.C. Mahalanobis.

example.q: Compare the First and Second Five Year Plans in a table.
steps: First Plan (1951-56): agriculture, dams, irrigation; K.N. Raj ('hasten slowly').
Second Plan (1956-61): rapid heavy industrialisation; P.C. Mahalanobis; tariffs to protect domestic industry.
example.answer: First: agriculture-led (K.N. Raj); Second: heavy industry-led (Mahalanobis)

learn.reallife: The Bhakra Nangal dam, which irrigates fields in Punjab and Haryana, and the Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur steel plants are symbols of the first two Plans.

topics.title: Public sector, import substitution and the mixed economy

learn.hook: India's early steel plants were built by the state, while textile mills and shops stayed private. That mix had a name: the mixed economy.
points: The public sector (industries owned by the government) was given a leading role in key areas such as steel, mining, power and heavy machinery.
Import substitution meant producing at home the goods that were earlier imported, protected by tariffs and controls on imports.
India adopted a mixed economy: both the public sector and the private sector existed, but the state played a major role in planning and in key industries.

Critics from the right said the state controlled too much, creating a licence-permit system and inefficiency. Critics from the left said the private sector and the rich gained too much, and the poor too little.
Exercise tip: compare the First and Second Plans, and explain the two models of development and why India chose a mixed path.

example.answer: An economy with both public and private sectors, with a key planning role for the state

chapters.title: Politics in India: India's External Relations

topics.title: India's foreign policy: context, Article 51 and Nehru's goals

learn.hook: India became free just as the Cold War split the world into two armed camps. A poor, newly independent country had to find its own way between them.
points: India became independent in a world shaped by the Cold War rivalry between the USA-led and USSR-led blocs. Newly independent India wanted to protect its freedom while building its economy.

Article 51 of the Constitution, a Directive Principle of State Policy, asks the state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
Jawaharlal Nehru was both Prime Minister and Foreign Minister from 1946 to 1964, and he played a central role in shaping India's foreign policy.
Nehru's three major objectives: to preserve the hard-earned sovereignty of the country, to protect its territorial integrity, and to promote rapid economic development.

example.q: Which part of the Constitution guides India's foreign policy towards peace, and what does it say?
steps: It is Article 51, in the Directive Principles of State Policy.
It asks the state to promote international peace and security and just relations between nations.

example.answer: Article 51: promote peace and security, just relations, respect for international law, settlement by arbitration

learn.reallife: When Indian diplomats call for dialogue and peaceful settlement at the UN, they are echoing the spirit of Article 51.

topics.title: Non-alignment and Afro-Asian unity

learn.hook: Choosing not to join either superpower's camp did not mean sitting on the fence. Non-alignment let India decide each issue on its merits.
points: Non-alignment meant keeping away from the military alliances of both the US-led and the Soviet-led blocs, while staying free to take an independent position on each issue.
Non-alignment was not isolation or neutrality: India took active stands, for example on decolonisation and disarmament, and developed relations with both blocs.
India championed Afro-Asian unity. Nehru convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi in March 1947, before independence.
The Afro-Asian conference at Bandung, Indonesia, in 1955 marked a high point of solidarity among newly independent countries and paved the way for the Non-Aligned Movement.
The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was held in Belgrade in September 1961. Nehru was a co-founder, along with Josip Broz Tito of Yugoslavia and Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt.

example.q: Order: First NAM summit; Asian Relations Conference; Bandung Conference.
steps: March 1947: Asian Relations Conference, New Delhi.
1955: Bandung Conference, Indonesia.
1961: First NAM summit, Belgrade.

learn.reallife: India still describes its foreign policy as one of 'strategic autonomy', a modern descendant of non-alignment.

topics.title: Panchsheel and the Tibet issue

learn.hook: In 1954 India and China agreed on five principles for living as good neighbours. Five years later, a young monk crossed the Himalayas into India, and the friendship began to strain.
points: Panchsheel, the five principles of peaceful coexistence, was signed by Nehru and Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954.

The five principles: mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty; mutual non-aggression; mutual non-interference in each other's internal affairs; equality and mutual benefit; and peaceful coexistence.
Tibet had historically been an area of friction. China took control of Tibet in 1950, and India did not openly oppose it.
In 1959 a rebellion broke out in Tibet. The Dalai Lama crossed into India and sought political asylum, which India granted. China strongly objected, and relations worsened.

example.answer: Territorial integrity and sovereignty; non-aggression; non-interference; equality and mutual benefit; peaceful coexistence

topics.title: The Chinese aggression of 1962 and after

learn.hook: In October 1962 Chinese troops attacked across the Himalayas. The short war shook India's confidence and changed its politics.
points: Border disputes, mainly over Aksai Chin in the Ladakh region and much of what was then NEFA (now Arunachal Pradesh), had grown after the 1950s.
In October 1962 China launched a swift and massive invasion on both disputed regions. India's forces were unprepared, and China declared a unilateral ceasefire after advancing.
The defeat hurt India's image and Nehru's standing. Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet. The first no-confidence motion against Nehru's government was moved in the Lok Sabha.
The war also affected domestic politics: differences over China contributed to the split in the Communist Party of India in 1964.

Normalisation took time: full diplomatic relations were restored in 1976. Atal Bihari Vajpayee visited China as External Affairs Minister in 1979, and Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit started a new phase of ties.

example.q: List two domestic consequences of the 1962 war in India.
steps: Defence Minister V.K. Krishna Menon had to leave the cabinet.

topics.title: Wars and peace with Pakistan: 1947-48 to 1965

learn.hook: Within weeks of independence, India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir. Yet in 1960 they signed a water treaty that survived the wars of 1965 and 1971.
points: Soon after independence, a conflict broke out over Kashmir in 1947-48, often described as a proxy war, when Pakistan backed armed raiders. It ended with a ceasefire, and the issue was taken to the UN.
Despite conflict, the two countries cooperated on some issues. The Indus Waters Treaty was signed in 1960 by Nehru and General Ayub Khan, with the World Bank's mediation.

In 1965 Pakistan launched armed attacks in the Rann of Kutch area of Gujarat in April, followed by a bigger offensive in Jammu and Kashmir in August-September. Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri ordered Indian forces to respond, and they advanced close to Lahore.
The war ended with UN intervention. The Tashkent Agreement was signed in January 1966 by Shastri and General Ayub Khan, brokered by the Soviet Union.

topics.title: The Bangladesh War of 1971 and the Kargil conflict

learn.hook: In December 1971, within about two weeks, India's forces helped create a new nation. Nearly three decades later, Indian soldiers fought on icy peaks in Kargil.
points: In 1970 East Pakistan voted overwhelmingly for the Awami League, but the West Pakistan leadership refused to accept the result. The Pakistani army began a crackdown in 1971, and about 80 lakh refugees fled to India.
India faced a hostile combination of the USA, Pakistan and China. To counter this, India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union in August 1971.

Full-scale war broke out in December 1971. Indian forces, with the support of local people, advanced quickly; within about ten days they had surrounded Dhaka, and the Pakistani army surrendered. Bangladesh became independent.
The Shimla Agreement between Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, signed in 1972, formalised the return of peace.
In 1999 Pakistani forces and militants occupied heights in the Kargil sector (including Mashkoh, Dras, Kaksar and Batalik). India responded strongly and recaptured the positions.

example.q: Why did India sign the Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the USSR in 1971?
steps: The USA and China were moving closer, with Pakistan's help.

example.answer: To counter the US-China-Pakistan combination during the Bangladesh crisis

topics.title: India's nuclear policy

learn.hook: Nehru called for the world to give up nuclear weapons. Decades later India tested its own. The story of India's nuclear policy is about principle meeting security.
points: Nehru had great faith in science and technology for building modern India, and he opposed nuclear weapons, pleading for comprehensive nuclear disarmament. The atomic energy programme was led by Homi J. Bhabha.

India conducted its first nuclear explosion at Pokhran in May 1974, calling it a peaceful nuclear explosion. In May 1998 India carried out a series of nuclear tests, and Pakistan tested soon afterwards.

India refused to sign the NPT (1968) and the CTBT (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, 1996), calling them discriminatory because they allow existing nuclear powers to keep their weapons while denying others.

India's nuclear doctrine: no first use (India will not be the first to use nuclear weapons) and credible minimum nuclear deterrence. India remains committed to global, verifiable and non-discriminatory nuclear disarmament.

chapters.title: Politics in India: Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System

topics.title: The challenge of political succession: Nehru to Shastri to Indira

learn.hook: Many new democracies collapsed when their founding leader died. When Nehru died in May 1964, the world watched to see whether India would too.
points: Nehru died in May 1964. Many feared a crisis of succession, but the transition was smooth: Lal Bahadur Shastri was chosen unanimously as the leader of the Congress parliamentary party and became Prime Minister.
Shastri was Prime Minister from 1964 to 1966. He faced food shortages and the 1965 war with Pakistan, and gave the famous slogan 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.

Shastri died suddenly at Tashkent in January 1966, soon after signing the Tashkent Agreement. The contest for leadership was between Morarji Desai and Indira Gandhi, and Indira Gandhi won in a secret ballot among Congress MPs, with more than two-thirds of their support.

The 'Syndicate' was an informal group of senior Congress leaders who controlled the party organisation. It was led by K. Kamaraj, Congress President, and included S.K. Patil, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy and Atulya Ghosh.
The Syndicate played a key role in choosing both Shastri and Indira Gandhi, and expected Indira to depend on its advice.

example.q: Why was the succession after Nehru's death considered a test for Indian democracy?
steps: Nehru had dominated politics since independence.
Many newly independent countries had seen turmoil or military takeover after a founding leader's death.
India's smooth transfer of power to Shastri, and then to Indira Gandhi, showed that its democratic institutions worked.
example.answer: Because a smooth transfer of power without crisis proved democracy's strength

topics.title: The fourth general election, 1967: a 'political earthquake'

learn.hook: In 1967 the Congress still won the Lok Sabha, but lost power in several states and saw many big leaders defeated. Observers called it a 'political earthquake'.
points: The period before 1967 was one of economic crisis: monsoon failure, widespread drought, a fall in agricultural production, serious food shortages, depletion of foreign exchange reserves, a drop in industrial production and exports, and higher military spending.
In June 1966 the government devalued the rupee, a step widely seen as taken under US pressure. Prices rose sharply, and protests spread.

Non-Congressism: Ram Manohar Lohia gave this strategy, arguing that the opposition parties should come together to defeat the Congress, which he saw as undemocratic and opposed to the interests of the poor.

Results of the 1967 election: the Congress got a majority in the Lok Sabha but with its lowest tally since 1952. Half the ministers in Indira Gandhi's cabinet and leaders like K. Kamaraj lost their seats. The Congress lost its majority in seven states, and in two more, defections prevented it from forming a government.

topics.title: Coalitions and defections after 1967

learn.hook: After 1967, parties that had little in common ideologically shared power in the states. And one MLA changed sides so often that he gave Indian politics a new phrase.
points: The 1967 elections brought coalition governments in many states. They were called Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments, meaning 'joint legislature party'.

These coalitions were ideologically varied. In Bihar the SVD government included the two socialist parties (SSP and PSP), the CPI on the left and the Jana Sangh on the right. In Punjab the 'Popular United Front' included the two rival Akali groups, the CPI, the CPI(M), the SSP, the Republican Party and the Jana Sangh.
Defection means an elected representative leaving the party on whose symbol he or she was elected and joining another party. Defections caused frequent rise and fall of state governments after 1967.
The phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' comes from Gaya Lal, an MLA in Haryana, who changed his party three times within a fortnight in 1967.
Defections were later checked by the anti-defection law, added to the Constitution in 1985.

example.q: Why were SVD governments in states unstable?
steps: They were coalitions of parties with very different ideologies.
Members often defected to other parties.
So disagreements and defections frequently brought them down.

topics.title: Indira Gandhi versus the Syndicate: the road to the split

learn.hook: In 1969 a sitting Prime Minister campaigned against her own party's official candidate for President, and won.
points: Indira Gandhi faced challenges from the Syndicate, which expected her to follow its advice. She gradually built her own independent position and tried to give the party a more radical, pro-poor image.

In 1967 the Congress Working Committee adopted a Ten-Point Programme, including social control of banks, nationalisation of general insurance, ceilings on urban property and income, public distribution of food grains, land reforms and house sites for the rural poor.
In 1969 President Zakir Hussain died. The Syndicate got N. Sanjeeva Reddy nominated as the official Congress candidate, despite Indira Gandhi's reservations.

Indira Gandhi encouraged the then Vice-President, V.V. Giri, to file his nomination as an independent. Just before the election she nationalised fourteen leading private banks (July 1969) and removed Morarji Desai as Finance Minister.
She called for a 'conscience vote', asking Congress MPs and MLAs to vote as they wished. V.V. Giri won, and the official Congress candidate lost.

V.V. Giri elected President (August 1969).

topics.title: The Congress splits; privy purses abolished

learn.hook: By late 1969 the party that had led the freedom struggle had broken into two. One side was called the 'Organisation', the other the 'Requisitionists'.
points: The defeat of the official candidate formalised the split. The Congress President, S. Nijalingappa, expelled Indira Gandhi from the party in November 1969.
The Congress split into two: the Congress (O), for 'Organisation', led by the Syndicate, and the Congress (R), for 'Requisitionists', led by Indira Gandhi.
Indira Gandhi presented the split as an ideological fight between socialists and conservatives, the pro-poor and the pro-rich.
Privy purses were grants paid by the government to the former rulers of princely states and their heirs, promised at the time of integration. Indira Gandhi supported their abolition.

Her government's attempt to amend the Constitution in 1970 failed in the Rajya Sabha, and its order 'de-recognising' the princes was struck down by the Supreme Court. Privy purses were finally abolished by a constitutional amendment after the 1971 election.

example.q: Explain the meaning of Congress (O) and Congress (R).

example.answer: Congress (O) = Organisation (Syndicate); Congress (R) = Requisitionists (Indira Gandhi)

topics.title: The 1971 election and the restoration of Congress dominance

learn.hook: The opposition's slogan was 'Indira hatao'. Her reply was 'Garibi hatao'. In 1971 voters chose the second by a landslide.
points: Indira Gandhi recommended dissolving the Lok Sabha in December 1970, and fresh elections were held in February 1971, ahead of schedule.

The non-communist, non-Congress opposition parties, including the Congress (O), formed a 'Grand Alliance' with the slogan 'Indira hatao' (remove Indira). Indira Gandhi offered a positive programme with the slogan 'Garibi hatao' (remove poverty).
The Congress (R) and CPI alliance won more seats and votes than the Congress had won in any of the first four elections. The Congress (R) alone won 352 seats, while the Congress (O) won only 16.

Restoration: the Congress system was restored, but it was different. The new Congress depended heavily on the popularity of a single leader, Indira Gandhi, and had fewer factions and a weaker organisation.

The victory in the Bangladesh war in December 1971 further raised Indira Gandhi's popularity, and the Congress swept the state assembly elections of 1972. Exam tip: order the events of 1964-71 by date.

example.q: Compare the restored Congress of 1971 with the old Congress system.
steps: Old system: coalition of many groups and factions, strong organisation, internal opposition.
Restored Congress: dominance built around one popular leader, Indira Gandhi.

example.answer: The restored Congress depended on one leader rather than a broad coalition of factions

chapters.title: Politics in India: The Crisis of Democratic Order

topics.title: Background to the Emergency: economic crisis and popular movements

learn.hook: Only three years after a historic election victory, students were protesting in Gujarat, Bihar was in turmoil, and the railways had ground to a halt.
points: Economic context: after 1971, the 'Garibi hatao' promise was not fulfilled. The costs of the Bangladesh crisis and refugees, the stopping of US aid, and a sharp rise in international oil prices in 1973 caused high inflation. Industrial growth was low and unemployment was high, especially among educated rural youth.

Gujarat movement (January 1974): students protested against rising prices of food grains, cooking oil and other essentials, and against corruption at high levels. Major opposition parties joined, President's rule was imposed, and Morarji Desai went on an indefinite fast demanding fresh elections. In June 1975 the Congress lost the assembly election.

Bihar movement (March 1974): students protesting against price rise, food scarcity, unemployment and corruption invited Jayaprakash Narayan (JP) to lead them. JP accepted on the condition that the movement remain non-violent and not be confined to Bihar.

JP gave the call for 'Total Revolution' (Sampoorna Kranti) to establish what he saw as true democracy. He demanded the dismissal of the Congress government in Bihar, and in 1975 led a people's march to Parliament, one of the largest political rallies ever held in the capital.

In May 1974 the National Coordination Committee for Railwaymen's Struggle, led by George Fernandes, called a nationwide railway strike for bonus and better service conditions. The government declared it illegal, and it was called off after twenty days.

example.q: List three developments of 1973-74 that added to tension before the Emergency.
steps: Rising prices after the 1973 oil price hike and economic slowdown.
Student-led movements in Gujarat and Bihar against price rise and corruption, with JP's call for Total Revolution.
The nationwide railway strike led by George Fernandes.
example.answer: Price rise, the Gujarat and Bihar movements, and the railway strike

learn.reallife: Patna's Gandhi Maidan and Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, sites of huge rallies in 1974-75, remain the stages for mass political gatherings today.

topics.title: Conflict with the judiciary and the Allahabad High Court verdict

learn.hook: On 12 June 1975, a High Court judge in Allahabad declared the Prime Minister's own election invalid. Within two weeks India was under Emergency.
points: The government and the ruling party had serious differences with the judiciary over whether Parliament could abridge Fundamental Rights, curtail the right to property, and amend the Constitution to give primacy to Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights.
In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), the Supreme Court ruled that Parliament could amend the Constitution but could not change its basic structure.

In 1973, when the post of Chief Justice of India fell vacant, the government set aside the convention of appointing the senior-most judge. It appointed Justice A.N. Ray, superseding three senior judges who had ruled against the government. This was criticised as an attack on judicial independence.

On 12 June 1975, Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha of the Allahabad High Court declared Indira Gandhi's election to the Lok Sabha invalid, on a petition filed by Raj Narain, a socialist leader who had contested against her in 1971.
On 24 June 1975 the Supreme Court granted a partial stay: she could remain an MP but could not take part in Lok Sabha proceedings until her appeal was decided.

example.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in the Kesavananda Bharati case?
steps: The question was how far Parliament could amend the Constitution.
The Court held that Parliament can amend the Constitution.
But it cannot alter the Constitution's basic structure.

topics.title: Declaration of Emergency and the government's response

learn.hook: On the night of 25 June 1975, newspaper offices lost their electricity, and before dawn hundreds of opposition leaders were arrested. India had entered the Emergency.
points: On 25 June 1975 the opposition held a massive rally in Delhi's Ramlila grounds, where JP called for nationwide protests and urged the army, police and government employees not to obey 'illegal and immoral orders'.

That night the government declared a national Emergency under Article 352, citing a threat of 'internal disturbance'. President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed issued the proclamation, and the cabinet was informed early the next morning.
Electricity to major newspaper offices was cut, and opposition leaders were arrested in large numbers. Press censorship was imposed: newspapers needed prior approval for what they published.
Organisations such as the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and the Jamaat-e-Islami were banned. Protests, strikes and public agitations were not allowed.

Preventive detention was widely used, mainly under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). In the ADM Jabalpur case (1976), the Supreme Court accepted the government's view that citizens could not move the courts for habeas corpus during the Emergency, a decision later widely criticised.

example.q: Under which article was the 1975 Emergency declared, and on what ground?
steps: The Constitution allows a national emergency under Article 352.
In 1975 the ground cited was 'internal disturbance'.
The President proclaimed it on 25 June 1975.
example.answer: Article 352, on the ground of internal disturbance

learn.reallife: Some newspapers, like The Indian Express and The Statesman, protested censorship by leaving blank spaces where censored news would have appeared.

topics.title: Consequences of the Emergency

learn.hook: Blank columns in newspapers, writers returning their awards, and more than a lakh people detained without trial: the Emergency touched almost every democratic institution.
points: Civil liberties were badly affected: fundamental rights were in effect suspended, people could not easily approach courts, and the press was censored. Some writers returned their awards in protest; for example, Kannada writer Shivarama Karanth returned his Padma Bhushan and Hindi writer Phanishwar Nath Renu returned his Padma Shri.
The independence of the judiciary was weakened, as rulings like ADM Jabalpur showed.

Constitutional changes: an amendment of 1975 (the 39th) declared that the elections of the Prime Minister, President and Vice-President could not be challenged in court. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made a whole series of changes: for example, it extended the term of the Lok Sabha and state assemblies from five to six years, and it limited the powers of the courts.
There were serious excesses: compulsory sterilisation drives and demolition of slums and jhuggis in places like Delhi, carried out forcibly.

After the Emergency, the Janata government appointed the Shah Commission (May 1977), headed by Justice J.C. Shah, a retired Chief Justice of India, to inquire into the excesses. It found that a very large number of people, over one lakh, had been arrested under preventive detention laws.

topics.title: Lessons of the Emergency

learn.hook: In 1977, voters who had been silenced for nearly two years used the ballot to speak. The Emergency taught India that democracy is not easily switched off.
points: The Emergency showed both the weaknesses and the strengths of Indian democracy. It proved that it is extremely difficult to do away with democracy in India: within about two years, democratic politics returned through elections.
It brought out ambiguities in the emergency provisions. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced the ground of 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' for a national emergency on internal grounds.
The 44th Amendment also made it necessary for the President to act on the written advice of the Council of Ministers when proclaiming an emergency.
The Emergency made people more aware of civil liberties. Many civil liberties organisations emerged afterwards.
It also highlighted the need for an independent judiciary and a police and bureaucracy that follow the law rather than the ruling party.

example.q: How did the 44th Amendment respond to the experience of 1975?
steps: In 1975, 'internal disturbance' had been a vague ground.
The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced it with 'armed rebellion'.
It also required the Council of Ministers' advice to the President to be in writing.
example.answer: It changed the ground to 'armed rebellion' and required written cabinet advice

learn.reallife: Organisations working on civil liberties and human rights in India, many of which grew after 1977, continue to monitor police and detention practices.

topics.title: Politics after the Emergency: the Janata experiment and its legacy

learn.hook: In March 1977 the Prime Minister lost her own seat, and for the first time a non-Congress government took charge in New Delhi.
points: In January 1977, the government announced elections and released opposition leaders. The major opposition parties came together to form the Janata Party, under the guidance of JP. Some Congress leaders opposed to the Emergency, such as Jagjivan Ram, left the Congress and formed the Congress for Democracy, which later merged with the Janata Party.

In the March 1977 Lok Sabha election, the Congress won only 154 seats, while the Janata Party and its allies won 330 of 542 seats. Indira Gandhi lost from Rae Bareli. The election was seen as a referendum on the Emergency.

Morarji Desai became Prime Minister, with Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram as rival claimants to the post. The Janata government lacked a common programme and clear leadership, and Morarji Desai's government lost its majority in 1979. Charan Singh then formed a government on the assurance of Congress support, but it lasted only a few months.
Fresh elections in January 1980 brought the Congress back to power under Indira Gandhi, with 353 seats.

Legacy: the 1977 election made anti-Congress politics a stronger force and saw the rise of backward-class politics, especially in north India. The Janata government appointed the Mandal Commission. Exam tip: list causes and consequences of the Emergency and evaluate its lessons.

example.q: Why did the Janata government collapse so quickly?

example.answer: Lack of a common programme and leadership rivalry

topics.title: Region and the nation: the Indian approach

learn.hook: India has hundreds of languages and many regions with distinct histories. Holding them together without flattening them is one of democracy's hardest jobs.
points: The Indian approach to diversity: regional aspirations are to be accommodated through democratic means. Unity is not seen as uniformity; regions are allowed to express their identity within the nation.

After independence, many regions voiced demands: some for autonomy or new states, some for special status, and a few for secession. The areas of greatest tension included Jammu and Kashmir, Punjab and the North-East, along with linguistic and regional movements elsewhere.
The Constitution provides flexible arrangements, such as reorganisation of states, special provisions for some regions, and autonomous councils for tribal areas.
The aim is to balance national unity and integrity with respect for regional diversity, so that regional aspirations strengthen rather than weaken democracy.

example.q: Explain the Indian approach to regional diversity in one line, and give an example.
steps: India accommodates regional demands through democratic negotiation, not suppression.

topics.title: Jammu and Kashmir: roots of the issue and early politics

learn.hook: In October 1947, armed raiders from across the new border moved towards Srinagar. The Maharaja's decision in those days shaped the region's future.
points: Jammu and Kashmir has three regions: Jammu, the Kashmir valley and Ladakh. Before 1947 it was a princely state ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh, who did not want to join either India or Pakistan.

In October 1947, Pakistan sent tribal infiltrators to capture Kashmir. The Maharaja asked India for military help. India sent its army, after the Maharaja signed the Instrument of Accession with India, and the infiltrators were driven back from the Kashmir valley.

External dispute: a part of the state remained under Pakistan's occupation, known in India as Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (POJK). Pakistan has claimed Kashmir, and the issue has been central to India-Pakistan conflicts.

Internal dispute: there were debates about the state's status within India. Article 370 gave the state special status and greater autonomy than other states, and some groups demanded still greater autonomy.

Sheikh Abdullah of the National Conference, a leader of the popular movement against the Maharaja, became Prime Minister of the state in 1948. He was dismissed in 1953 and kept in detention for years. After an agreement with Indira Gandhi in 1974, he became Chief Minister.

topics.title: Jammu and Kashmir: insurgency, elections and the 2019 change

learn.hook: On 5 August 2019, Parliament changed the constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir. The decision came after decades of militancy, elections and coalition politics.
points: Farooq Abdullah succeeded his father as Chief Minister after 1982. The 1987 assembly election was won by the National Conference-Congress alliance, but many believed the election did not reflect the people's choice.

From 1989 the state saw a militant movement, supported from across the border, that demanded a separate Kashmiri nation or merger with Pakistan. The state was under President's rule for several years, and violence caused great suffering, including the displacement of Kashmiri Pandits from the valley.

Elections were held again in 1996. In 2002 the National Conference lost, and a coalition of the People's Democratic Party (PDP) and the Congress formed the government under Mufti Mohammad Sayeed. Later elections produced other coalition governments, including a PDP-BJP coalition after 2014.

On 5 August 2019, the provisions of Article 370 that gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir were abrogated. Under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the state was reorganised into two Union Territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

topics.title: Punjab: from Punjabi Suba to the Punjab Accord

learn.hook: Punjab went from being a hub of the Green Revolution to a decade of violence, and then back to peace. Its story shows both the dangers and the healing power of democracy.
points: The Akali Dal, formed in 1920 as the political wing of the Sikhs, led the movement for a 'Punjabi Suba'. In 1966 Punjab was reorganised: Haryana was carved out of it as a new state, and its hill areas were merged with Himachal Pradesh. The Akali Dal came to power in 1967 and in 1977, in coalition governments.
In 1973 the Akali Dal passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution. It asserted regional autonomy and wanted to redefine centre-state relations in India, and spoke of the aspirations of the Sikh community.

A cycle of violence followed: militant groups demanded a separate Sikh state and made the Golden Temple in Amritsar their headquarters. In June 1984 the Government of India carried out 'Operation Blue Star', an army operation to remove militants from the Golden Temple, which deeply hurt Sikh sentiments.

On 31 October 1984, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by her bodyguards. Large-scale violence against the Sikh community followed in Delhi and many parts of north India, in which thousands were killed.

Road to peace: in July 1985 Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and Harchand Singh Longowal, the Akali Dal president, signed the Punjab Accord. Violence continued for some years, but by the mid-1990s normalcy returned and elections restored democratic politics.

topics.title: The North-East: autonomy, new states and secessionist movements

learn.hook: A strip of land only about 22 km wide links the North-East to the rest of India. Beyond it lie seven states with remarkable diversity.
points: The North-East has seven states, called the 'seven sisters': Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. It is home to about 4 per cent of India's population and is linked to the rest of India by a narrow corridor about 22 km wide.
The region borders China, Myanmar, Bangladesh and Bhutan. It has great ethnic and linguistic diversity, and its relative isolation and lack of development caused grievances.

Demands for autonomy: at independence, most of the region was part of Assam. Non-Assamese groups felt the Assamese language was being imposed, and tribal leaders demanded separation. Over time Nagaland (1963), Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura (1972), and Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh (1987) became states.

Mizo movement: after a famine in 1959 that people felt the Assam government had not handled well, the Mizo National Front (MNF) under Laldenga began an armed struggle for independence in 1966. After two decades, Rajiv Gandhi and Laldenga signed the Mizoram Accord in 1986. Mizoram became a full state, and Laldenga became Chief Minister.

Naga movement: under Angami Zapu Phizo, a section of Nagas declared independence from India on 14 August 1947 and launched an armed struggle. Nagaland became a state in 1963, but the Naga issue has continued to be negotiated.

example.q: How did the Mizo insurgency end, and why is it cited as a success?

example.answer: Through the 1986 Mizoram Accord; insurgents joined democratic politics

topics.title: The Assam movement and national integration

learn.hook: From 1979 to 1985, students in Assam led one of the longest mass movements in independent India, on the question of who is an outsider.
points: Movements against 'outsiders' arose in the North-East because large-scale migration was seen as a threat by local communities, who feared becoming a minority and losing jobs, land and political power.

The Assam Movement (1979-1985) was led by the All Assam Students' Union (AASU), a students' group. It demanded that illegal migrants, mainly from Bangladesh, be identified and sent back, and that their names be removed from voters' lists. The movement had wide support and was largely non-violent, though there were incidents of violence.

In 1985 the Rajiv Gandhi government and the AASU leaders signed the Assam Accord. Foreigners who had migrated to Assam during and after the Bangladesh war (that is, from 1971) were to be identified and deported.
After the accord, the AASU leaders formed a political party, the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP), which came to power in Assam in 1985 with Prafulla Kumar Mahanta as Chief Minister.
The Assam case shows that even very difficult issues can be addressed through democratic negotiation, though the problem of migration has not been fully resolved.

topics.title: Accommodation and national integration: the lessons

learn.hook: Rebels who became Chief Ministers, autonomy councils in tribal hills, and new states on the map: India's regional story has many lessons.
points: Lesson 1: regional aspirations are a part of democratic politics. Expressing regional issues is not abnormal or anti-national.
Lesson 2: the best way to respond is through democratic negotiation rather than suppression. Accords in Punjab, Mizoram and Assam show this.
Lesson 3: power sharing matters. Regions and groups need a real share in decision-making at the state and national levels.
Lesson 4: regional imbalance in economic development can feed feelings of discrimination, so balanced development is necessary.

Lesson 5: the Constitution's flexibility, such as special provisions and the Sixth Schedule's autonomous councils for tribal areas, helps accommodate diversity. Exam tip: practise matching movements with their leaders and accords, and map work on these regions.

example.q: Match each accord with its leaders: Punjab Accord, Mizoram Accord, Assam Accord.

Assam Accord (1985): Rajiv Gandhi government and AASU leaders.

chapters.title: Politics in India: Recent Developments in Indian Politics

topics.title: The context of the 1990s

learn.hook: Between 1989 and 1992, India saw a hung Parliament, a former Prime Minister assassinated, an economic crisis and the biggest caste and religious mobilisations in decades. The decade reshaped Indian politics.
points: In 1984, after Indira Gandhi's assassination, Rajiv Gandhi led the Congress to a massive victory. But in 1989 the Congress lost its majority, ending the era of Congress dominance often called the 'Congress system'.
Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated on 21 May 1991, during the election campaign, by members of the LTTE. After the election, P.V. Narasimha Rao became Prime Minister.

Key developments of the period: the defeat of the Congress in 1989 and the end of the Congress system; the Mandal issue (1990), which brought backward-caste politics to the centre; the New Economic Policy of 1991, which began economic reforms; and the Ayodhya movement, which culminated in the events of December 1992.
These developments led to multi-party competition at the national level. No single party could easily win a majority, and coalition governments became common.

example.q: List four developments of 1989-1992 that changed Indian politics.
steps: End of the Congress system after the 1989 election.

learn.reallife: Many of today's major regional parties, from Bihar to Tamil Nadu, became powerful national players in the coalition politics that began in this period.

topics.title: The era of coalitions: National Front and United Front

learn.hook: From December 1989 to March 1998, six different leaders served as Prime Minister. Parties that had fought each other in elections propped up governments from outside.
points: In the 1989 election, the Congress emerged as the largest party but was far short of a majority. The National Front, an alliance of the Janata Dal and some regional parties, formed the government under V.P. Singh.
The National Front government received support from two very different sides: the BJP and the Left Front, both from outside the government. It lasted less than a year, after the BJP withdrew support.
In 1996, after a short-lived BJP government, the United Front, a coalition of regional and other non-Congress, non-BJP parties, formed the government with Congress support from outside.
The United Front Prime Ministers were H.D. Deve Gowda (1996-97) and I.K. Gujral (1997-98).
These governments showed that coalitions could bring regional parties to the centre of national power, but also that outside support made governments unstable.

topics.title: NDA and UPA: coalitions become the norm

learn.hook: From 1989 to 2014, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority on its own. Governing meant building alliances.
points: In 1998 the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) formed the government under Atal Bihari Vajpayee. It lost a confidence vote in 1999, but returned to power after the 1999 election and ruled until 2004.

In 2004 the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA) formed the government, with Manmohan Singh as Prime Minister. The UPA won again in 2009, and Manmohan Singh was Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014.
From 1989 to 2014, coalition and alliance governments were the norm at the Centre. Both national parties had to share power with state-level and regional parties.
Coalition politics made bargaining and accommodation central to government. Alliances were often formed on practical, pragmatic grounds rather than shared ideology.

topics.title: The political rise of the Other Backward Classes: Mandal and after

learn.hook: In August 1990 a government decision on reservations sparked protests across north India and changed the shape of Indian politics for decades.
points: The Janata Party government set up the Second Backward Classes Commission in 1978 (announced in December 1978 and formally appointed on 1 January 1979), chaired by B.P. Mandal; it is known as the Mandal Commission. It submitted its report in 1980.

The Commission recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for the Other Backward Classes (OBCs). It also made other recommendations, such as land reform, to improve their conditions.

In August 1990, the National Front government under V.P. Singh decided to implement the recommendation of 27 per cent reservation for OBCs in central government jobs. This led to violent protests in many cities, especially by students opposed to the decision.

In the Indra Sawhney case (1992), the Supreme Court upheld OBC reservation, with conditions such as excluding the better-off sections (the 'creamy layer') and keeping overall reservations within limits.

Political fallout: OBC and Dalit-based parties grew. The Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), founded by Kanshi Ram in 1984, came to power in Uttar Pradesh in 1995. Other parties with strong OBC support also became powerful in north India.

example.q: Summarise the Mandal story in four steps.
steps: 1978: Mandal Commission set up by the Janata government.
1980: report recommends 27% reservation for OBCs.
1990: V.P. Singh government implements it in central jobs; protests follow.
1992: Supreme Court upholds it in the Indra Sawhney case.
example.answer: Commission (1978) → report (1980) → implementation (1990) → Indra Sawhney (1992)

topics.title: Ram Janmabhoomi movement, the 2019 verdict and the temple

learn.hook: One site in Ayodhya was at the centre of a legal and political debate for decades, until a unanimous Supreme Court verdict in 2019 settled the dispute.
points: The Ram Janmabhoomi movement sought the construction of a Ram temple at the site in Ayodhya believed by many Hindus to be the birthplace of Lord Ram. In 1986 a Faizabad district court ordered the opening of the locks of the structure at the site. The movement grew into a major national issue, and the BJP made it a central part of its politics.
In 1990, BJP leader L.K. Advani led a Rath Yatra from Somnath in Gujarat towards Ayodhya to build public support for the movement.

On 6 December 1992, the three-domed structure at the disputed site was demolished by people who had gathered there. This was followed by communal violence in several parts of the country, and some state governments were dismissed.

The dispute went through a long legal process. On 9 November 2019, a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court gave a unanimous verdict: the disputed land was to be given to a trust for building a Ram temple, and five acres of land elsewhere in Ayodhya were to be given for a mosque.

The verdict was accepted peacefully across the country, showing the strength of the legal process in resolving disputes. Construction of the Ram temple at the site began in 2020, and its consecration (pran pratishtha) ceremony was held in January 2024.

topics.title: Emergence of a new consensus

learn.hook: In 2014, for the first time since 1984, a single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha on its own. Yet many ideas that grew in the coalition era were shared across parties.
points: Lok Sabha elections from 2004 to 2019: the Congress-led UPA won in 2004 and 2009. In 2014 the BJP won a majority on its own (282 seats), the first time any party had done so since 1984, and it formed the government with its NDA allies under Narendra Modi. In 2019 the BJP won an even larger majority (303 seats). (In 2024 the BJP won 240 seats, short of a majority on its own, and the NDA formed the government with its allies, again under Narendra Modi.)
A growing consensus emerged among most parties on four points. First, agreement on the new economic policies: most parties support economic reforms, even if they differ on details.
Second, acceptance of the political and social claims of the backward castes: almost all parties support reservation for backward classes and seek their support.
Third, acceptance of the role of state-level parties in national governance: the line between regional and national parties has become less important.

Fourth, emphasis on pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions: alliances are often made without full ideological agreement. Exercise tip: explain the political impact of Mandal and order the coalition governments by date.

example.q: Name the four elements of the new consensus in Indian politics.
steps: Agreement on new economic policies.

Acceptance of the role of state-level parties in national governance.

example.answer: Economic policy; backward-caste claims; role of state parties; pragmatism over ideology

Answer: Acceptance of the political and social claims of backward castes

quiz.q: The new consensus includes an emphasis on:
options: Pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions
Strict ideological purity in all alliances
quiz.explain: Alliances are often formed on practical grounds.
steps: Asked: what the consensus emphasises in alliances.
Fact: alliances are often made without full ideological agreement.
That is pragmatism rather than ideological positions.
Answer: Pragmatic considerations rather than ideological positions

quiz.q: What does the consensus say about state-level parties?
options: Their role in national governance is accepted
quiz.explain: State parties became key partners at the Centre.
steps: Asked: the consensus view of state-level parties.
Fact: state parties became key partners at the Centre.
So their role in national governance is accepted.
Answer: Their role in national governance is accepted

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Most major parties now support economic reforms. Reason (R): Agreement on new economic policies is part of the new consensus.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the consensus on economic policy explains the broad support.
steps: A: true — most major parties support economic reforms.
R: true — agreement on new economic policies is part of the consensus.
R explains A: the consensus explains the broad support.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: By how many seats did the BJP's own tally rise from 2014 to 2019?
steps: Answer: 21
quiz.mistake: Adds the tallies or slips by ten

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'After all those coalitions, do parties agree on anything now?'
teach.praise: Cool! The BJP won majorities in 2014 and 2019, and most parties now agree on economic reforms, backward-caste claims, the role of state parties and pragmatic alliances!
teach.nudge: Good. What are the four points of the new consensus?

revise.summary: The UPA won in 2004 and 2009. In 2014 the BJP won 282 seats, the first single-party majority since 1984, and 303 in 2019. A new consensus formed on economic reforms, backward-caste claims, the role of state parties, and pragmatism over ideology.
focus: The four points of the new consensus
remember: BJP: 282 seats in 2014, 303 in 2019
First single-party majority since 1984
Consensus: reforms, backward castes, state parties, pragmatism
traps: Do not swap 282 (2014) and 303 (2019)
303 − 282 = 21 seats more, not 585
